title: A transfusion reaction after surgery

objective: Tell transfusion reactions apart: febrile nonhemolytic is most common, allergic reactions are often mild, acute hemolytic reactions come from ABO mismatch, and circulatory overload from excess volume
secondaryObjectives: Before a transfusion, verify the order, check for any premedication and relevant labs, ask about past reactions, and confirm a working IV with blood tubing and normal saline ready
Collect only one unit of blood from the bank at a time, and verify client identity, order, consent, blood type and compatibility at the bedside before starting

brief.situation: 10:00 on an orthopedic unit. Room 8, Mrs. Hughes, 74, day 1 after a hip replacement. Hemoglobin 7.0 this morning, dizzy when she stood. One unit of red cells is ordered over 2 hours. The unit has just arrived from the blood bank.
handover: No previous transfusions, no known reactions. Consent for blood was signed before surgery.
One 20-gauge IV in the left forearm, saline-locked.

Policy: two licensed staff check the client and the unit at the bedside; baseline vital signs before starting; stay with the client and run it slowly for the first 15 minutes; vital signs at 15 minutes.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Prepare and start the transfusion, then watch her. Some steps take a few minutes.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends at 11:15, then a debrief scores what you did.

which.question: Which kind of transfusion reaction is this most likely to be, how do you tell it from the others, and what do you do now?

parts.label: Which reaction
parts.criteria: Names an acute hemolytic reaction (ABO incompatibility) from chills and fever with back pain, anxiety, falling BP, rising HR and dark urine within minutes of starting; contrasts it with febrile nonhemolytic (fever and chills without hypotension or hemolysis), allergic (hives, itch) and circulatory overload (dyspnea, crackles, high BP).
parts.modelAnswer: An acute hemolytic reaction: chills, fever, sudden anxiety and back pain minutes in, with the pressure falling, the heart rate rising and dark urine. A febrile nonhemolytic reaction gives fever and chills without hypotension or hemolysis; an allergic one gives hives and itch; overload gives breathlessness, crackles and a high BP.

parts.label: What now
parts.criteria: Stops the transfusion at once and disconnects the blood tubing without flushing it; keeps IV access with new tubing and 0.9% saline; vital signs; notifies the provider and the blood bank; rechecks identity and labels; sends blood and urine samples with the bag and tubing; monitors urine output; never restarts the unit.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop it now and disconnect the blood tubing at the hub without flushing; new tubing with saline to keep the vein open; vital signs; call the provider and the blood bank; recheck the band and the tag; send blood and urine with the bag and tubing; watch the urine output and color. The unit is not restarted.

Start slowly and stay at the bedside.

shock.headline: Shock and DIC
shock.body: The amount of incompatible blood decides how bad hemolysis gets. Find the first sign in the log and when the unit was stopped, and whether a flush pushed the line's contents in.

stopped.headline: Caught in minutes
stopped.body: Prepared properly, started slowly and stayed, stopped at the first sign without flushing the line, and the right people told. That is the expert path.

stoppedLate.headline: Stopped, by a slower route
stoppedLate.body: She is being treated, but check when it was stopped, what was tried first, whether the line was flushed or the unit restarted, and when the provider and blood bank heard.

time_up.headline: Still running
time_up.body: Any new symptom during a transfusion means stop first and work out the cause after.

scoring.modelReasoning: Chills, fever, sudden anxiety and back pain within minutes of starting red cells, with a falling blood pressure, rising heart rate and dark urine, is an acute hemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility until proven otherwise. Febrile nonhemolytic reactions are the most common but do not cause hypotension or hemolysis; allergic reactions bring hives and itch; circulatory overload brings dyspnea, crackles and a high blood pressure. For any suspected reaction: stop the transfusion at once, disconnect the blood tubing without flushing it, keep IV access with new tubing and 0.9% saline, check vital signs, notify the provider and the blood bank, recheck the identity checks, send blood and urine samples with the bag and tubing, and watch the urine output. The unit is never restarted. Starting slowly and staying for the first 15 minutes is what makes an early stop possible.

noFlush.ask: While the provider calls back: why disconnect the blood tubing instead of flushing it?

choices.label: A flush pushes the red cells left in the tubing into her

noFlush.explain: The tubing still holds red cells from the incompatible unit; flushing pushes them in. Keep access with new tubing and saline instead.

whyCheck.ask: During the bedside check: what is the most common cause of an ABO-incompatible transfusion?

choices.label: Misidentification of the client or the sample
A wrong group printed by the lab analyzer

whyCheck.explain: Identification errors, at the bedside or when the crossmatch sample was drawn. That is why two people check the band against the tag and record, and why a check that passes cannot rule out a sample drawn from the wrong client.

whenReact.ask: While it runs: when do the severe acute reactions usually show?

choices.label: In the first 15 minutes or so
Near the end of the unit

whenReact.explain: Early: severe reactions often start within the first 15 minutes, which is why the first 15 minutes are run slowly with the nurse present. Delayed reactions can come days later.
